summary: Describes a file transfer service for the Internet that uses Telnet for option negotiation and the Kermit protocol for transferring and managing files. It is an informational memo.

eli5.summary: Kermit is an old way to send files between computers. This describes how to use it over the Internet by starting with a Telnet connection.

questions: how does internet kermit service work
subtitle: A file transfer service combining Telnet option negotiation with Kermit protocol.

tldr.problem: FTP requires multiple TCP connections and does not work well through firewalls and network address translators. Users also lose access to Kermit's powerful scripting, character-set translation, and file management features when used over a traditional Telnet connection.
tldr.mechanism: Internet Kermit Service (IKS) runs on a standard Telnet connection (port 1649), multiplexing option negotiation and Kermit protocol messages over a single channel. This provides file transfer and management, with optional authentication via Telnet options or TLS.
tldr.outcome: A file transfer service accessible from any Telnet client, supporting both authenticated and anonymous access, with firewall traversal, automation via scripts, and features FTP lacks such as character-set translation and flexible file selection.

facts.value: Kerberos 4/5, SRP, NTLM, TLS certificates, plaintext

today: RFC 2839 is an informational specification and has not been obsoleted. Internet Kermit Service was implemented in Columbia University's C-Kermit 7.0 and remains available, though it has not achieved the widespread deployment of FTP.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Internet Kermit Service (IKS) provides file transfer and management on the Internet using two existing standards: Telnet for connection and option negotiation, and the Kermit protocol for file transfer. Unlike FTP, which requires opening additional TCP connections and has historically been problematic for firewall traversal, IKS uses a single Telnet connection for both control and data transfer.

The service offers direct access to Kermit file transfer without requiring users to first establish a shell login. It supports both authenticated users and anonymous access, with Telnet options for authentication (Kerberos, SRP, NTLM) and encryption (TLS). All Telnet clients that support Kermit protocol, whether or not they support the specialized Telnet Kermit Option, can use IKS.
sections.eli5: IKS lets you send files to a remote computer using a Telnet connection, instead of needing FTP. One connection does everything instead of opening multiple connections.

sections.title: History and Motivation
sections.content:
The Kermit protocol was developed at Columbia University in 1981 to transfer files reliably between diverse computer types over potentially unreliable communication links. Unlike FTP, Kermit was designed for hostile environments and includes features like character-set translation, error recovery, and scripting capabilities. Kermit software is available for nearly every computer and operating system.

While Kermit has been widely used in academia, government, and business, it has never had a strong explicit connection to the Internet as a standard file transfer service. Users on the Internet would like to access Kermit's features—especially automation through scripts—but FTP is the standard. IKS fills this gap by providing Kermit functionality as an Internet service, preserving compatibility with existing Telnet clients while offering features FTP lacks, such as transfer through firewalls on a single port and character-set translation.
sections.eli5: Kermit was invented long ago for transferring files reliably. Internet Kermit Service brings these capabilities to the Internet alongside modern connection technology.

sections.title: The Internet Kermit Service Model
sections.content:
IKS listens on a standard TCP port (1649, assigned by IANA) and presents a Telnet interface. The key difference from a standard Telnet server is that IKS does not offer an interactive system shell; it provides only file transfer and management functions. The service negotiates Telnet options, including the Telnet Kermit Option, which determines how client and server coordinate their states.

Depending on Telnet Kermit Option negotiation, three configurations are possible. In Server-Side Kermit Server (SKS), the IKS is the Kermit server and accepts commands from a Kermit client. In Client-Side Kermit Server (CKS), the Telnet client is the Kermit server and the IKS issues a command prompt. In No Kermit Server (NKS), neither side explicitly controls the other; loose coupling characterizes the session. These configurations may change dynamically during a session via Telnet option subnegotiations.
sections.eli5: The IKS decides who is in charge during a session—either the server controls the transfer, the client controls it, or they work loosely together—and can switch modes during the connection.

sections.title: Authentication and Encryption
sections.content:
IKS supports multiple authentication methods. The Telnet AUTHENTICATION option allows use of Kerberos 4, Kerberos 5, Secure Remote Password, and Microsoft NTLM, eliminating the need to transmit passwords in plaintext. The Telnet START_TLS option provides TLS 1.0 encryption and X.509 certificate-based server and optional client authentication.

For backward compatibility with clients that do not support Telnet authentication options, IKS supports plaintext authentication via Kermit REMOTE LOGIN commands or interactive username/password prompts. However, these methods should only be used after negotiating Telnet START_TLS to prevent password sniffing. Anonymous login is supported, with access restricted to designated file system areas on UNIX systems. Encryption options include the Telnet Encryption option (supporting DES, CAST128, CAST5-40) and TLS.
sections.eli5: The connection can be secured in multiple ways: using encryption from Telnet, using TLS, or using strong authentication methods like Kerberos. If you can't use those, plaintext passwords should only be sent over encrypted connections.

sections.title: Services and User Interface
sections.content:
IKS provides extensive file transfer and management capabilities. Users can send or receive files with flexible selection using patterns, date ranges, size ranges, exception lists, and more. Files can be transferred in text or binary mode, with automatic switching per file. The service supports filename conversion, directory creation, atomic file movement (deleting or renaming only after successful transfer), attribute preservation (timestamps, permissions), and recovery of interrupted transfers.

A powerful feature inherited from Kermit is character-set translation during text-mode transfers, unique among mainstream file transfer protocols. Administrative features include configurable access controls, feature disabling (file reception, deletion, directory changes, etc.), and session logging. Kermit's script language enables automation with variables, arrays, functions, control structures, and procedure calls. Users can script complex file transfer workflows, or limit access to safe subsets of commands for anonymous users.
sections.eli5: IKS is more flexible than FTP. You can select files by date or size, convert character sets, automate transfers with scripts, and preserve file details like modification times.
